title: Heart Failure: Congestion, Perfusion, and Escalation
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: In heart failure, trend congestion and perfusion rather than treating edema as an isolated finding. New dyspnea at rest, falling oxygenation, chest pain, hypotension, confusion, or reduced urine output signals decompensation and requires rapid escalation.
recognize: Congestion clues include orthopnea, crackles, edema, jugular venous distention, rapid weight gain, and worsening exertional dyspnea.
Poor perfusion may appear as cool extremities, hypotension, confusion, weakness, or reduced urine output.
A rapid change matters more than a chronically abnormal baseline.
priorities: Position for easier breathing and assess respiratory effort and oxygenation.
Obtain vital signs, lung sounds, edema, weight trend, and urine output.
Report acute respiratory distress or poor-perfusion findings immediately.
assessMonitor: Daily weight at the same time and under similar conditions when ordered.
Trend intake/output, edema, lung sounds, oxygenation, blood pressure, heart rate, and medication response.
Monitor renal function and electrolytes when diuretics or renin-angiotensin system drugs are used.
interventions: Administer prescribed diuretics and other heart-failure medications and evaluate response.
Support sodium/fluid plan as ordered.
Promote energy conservation while avoiding unnecessary prolonged bed rest.
medicationSafety: Loop diuretics can cause volume depletion, hypokalemia, and renal dysfunction.
ACE inhibitors/ARBs/ARNI can cause hypotension, hyperkalemia, and renal changes.
Do not give routine oxygen solely for heart failure if the patient is not hypoxemic or in respiratory distress unless specifically ordered.
redFlags: Hypotension with cool skin or confusion
teaching: Teach daily weights, medication adherence, symptom reporting, sodium awareness, and when rapid weight gain or worsening dyspnea requires contact.
Reinforce smoking cessation and follow-up plan.
delegationScope: Routine weights and intake/output may be delegated with clear parameters for reporting.
The PN interprets trends within scope and reports acute changes; unstable cardiopulmonary assessment should be escalated to the RN/provider/rapid-response system.
examTrap: Focusing only on ankle edema while ignoring new confusion, hypotension, or decreasing urine output.
oneLinePearl: Heart failure is two questions: Is the patient wet, and are they perfusing?
sourceBasis: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure

title: Chest Pain and Suspected Acute Coronary Syndrome
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: New ischemic-type chest discomfort or an anginal equivalent is an emergency until evaluated. The PN's role is rapid recognition, immediate assessment, emergency-system activation/escalation, and ordered supportive care—not delaying for a complete routine history.
recognize: Pressure, heaviness, squeezing, dyspnea, diaphoresis, nausea, unexplained fatigue, or epigastric discomfort may represent ischemia.
Women, older adults, and people with diabetes may have less typical symptoms.
A normal initial ECG or early troponin does not by itself exclude acute coronary syndrome.
priorities: Stop activity and assess ABCs, vital signs, pain characteristics, and oxygenation.
Activate the emergency response and obtain a 12-lead ECG promptly when available.
Administer prescribed acute medications after checking contraindications.
assessMonitor: Monitor rhythm, blood pressure, oxygenation, level of consciousness, and symptom evolution.
Watch for heart failure, dysrhythmia, shock, or recurrent pain.
interventions: Keep the patient at rest and prepare for urgent transfer or higher-level care.
Follow facility protocol for aspirin or nitroglycerin when ordered/authorized and contraindications are absent.
medicationSafety: Nitroglycerin can worsen hypotension and is contraindicated with recent phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor use and in selected preload-dependent states.
Routine oxygen is not indicated for a normoxemic, non-distressed patient solely because chest pain is present.
redFlags: ST-segment elevation or dynamic ischemic changes
teaching: Teach that symptoms can recur and that emergency evaluation is required even if pain improves spontaneously.
delegationScope: Do not delegate assessment of new chest pain to unlicensed personnel.
The PN initiates emergency actions within policy and immediately escalates to the RN/provider/EMS pathway.
examTrap: Applying oxygen automatically to every chest-pain patient instead of first assessing oxygenation and respiratory distress.
oneLinePearl: New chest pressure is a clock-starting event, not a routine assessment task.
sourceBasis: 2025 ACC/AHA Guideline for Acute Coronary Syndromes

title: Atrial Fibrillation: Rate, Perfusion, and Stroke Risk
bottomLine: With atrial fibrillation, first determine whether the patient is stable. New hypotension, ischemic chest pain, severe dyspnea, syncope, or altered mentation suggests hemodynamic instability and requires urgent escalation.
recognize: Pulse may be irregularly irregular and ventricular rate may be rapid or controlled.
Symptoms range from none to palpitations, fatigue, dyspnea, dizziness, or chest discomfort.
Atrial fibrillation increases thromboembolic stroke risk.
priorities: Assess blood pressure, perfusion, respiratory status, chest pain, neurologic status, and heart rate/rhythm.
Escalate immediately if unstable.
Administer prescribed rate-control or anticoagulant therapy and monitor response.
assessMonitor: Monitor rhythm/rate, blood pressure, bleeding risk if anticoagulated, and signs of heart failure or stroke.
Review potassium and magnesium abnormalities when ordered.
interventions: Reduce exertion during symptomatic rapid rates.
Prepare for higher-level evaluation when the rhythm is new, symptomatic, or poorly controlled.
medicationSafety: Beta blockers and nondihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers may cause bradycardia or hypotension.
Anticoagulants reduce stroke risk but increase bleeding risk; report head injury or significant bleeding urgently.
teaching: Teach pulse awareness, medication adherence, anticoagulant safety, stroke warning signs, and when palpitations require urgent care.
delegationScope: Routine vital signs may be delegated with reporting parameters in stable patients.
Interpretation of a new irregular rhythm or new neurologic symptoms requires licensed-nurse assessment and escalation.
examTrap: Treating the heart-rate number before checking whether the patient is unstable or having stroke symptoms.
oneLinePearl: In AF, stability comes before rate control.

title: DVT and Pulmonary Embolism: Recognize the Escalation
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: A unilateral swollen painful leg suggests DVT; sudden unexplained dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, hypoxemia, syncope, or hemoptysis raises concern for pulmonary embolism. Suspected PE requires urgent escalation, not ambulation or massage.
recognize: DVT often causes unilateral swelling, warmth, tenderness, or erythema but may be subtle.
PE may present with sudden dyspnea, tachypnea, pleuritic pain, tachycardia, anxiety, hypoxemia, syncope, or hemoptysis.
Risk increases with immobility, surgery, trauma, cancer, estrogen exposure, pregnancy/postpartum, and prior VTE.
priorities: Stop activity and assess ABCs for suspected PE.
Escalate urgently and prepare for oxygen/supportive care if hypoxemic or distressed.
For suspected DVT, avoid massaging the limb and report promptly.
assessMonitor: Monitor respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, blood pressure, heart rate, chest symptoms, leg findings, and bleeding if anticoagulated.
interventions: Apply prescribed mechanical prophylaxis correctly when not contraindicated.
Promote early mobility when appropriate for prevention.
Administer anticoagulants as ordered and monitor for bleeding.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulants increase bleeding risk.
Thrombolytic therapy is reserved for selected high-risk situations and requires acute-care monitoring.
redFlags: New unilateral leg swelling plus dyspnea
teaching: Teach mobility, hydration as appropriate, adherence to anticoagulation, bleeding precautions, and urgent PE warning signs.
delegationScope: Routine mobility may be delegated for stable patients after the plan is established.
A new unilateral swollen leg or sudden respiratory symptom requires licensed-nurse evaluation and escalation.
examTrap: Massaging a painful swollen calf to improve circulation.
oneLinePearl: Swollen leg plus sudden dyspnea: think clot migration and escalate.
sourceBasis: American Society of Hematology VTE Guidelines

title: COPD Exacerbation: Ventilation, Oxygen, and Fatigue
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: In COPD exacerbation, treat hypoxemia while watching ventilation and work of breathing. Do not withhold needed oxygen because of the outdated fear that oxygen will simply 'remove the drive to breathe.'
recognize: Worsening dyspnea, increased sputum volume or purulence, wheezing, tachypnea, and increased work of breathing suggest exacerbation.
Drowsiness, confusion, silent chest, exhaustion, or worsening hypercapnia suggest impending respiratory failure.
priorities: Position upright and assess respiratory effort, oxygenation, mental status, and breath sounds.
Administer titrated oxygen to the prescribed target and bronchodilators as ordered.
Escalate if the patient is tiring, becoming confused, or failing to improve.
assessMonitor: Trend oxygen saturation, respiratory rate, ability to speak, accessory-muscle use, mental status, and response to bronchodilator therapy.
ABGs or venous gases may be used in acute care when hypercapnia or acidosis is suspected.
interventions: Encourage pursed-lip breathing when the patient can participate.
Cluster care to reduce oxygen demand during severe dyspnea.
Support prescribed noninvasive ventilation in appropriate monitored settings.
medicationSafety: Short-acting bronchodilators can cause tachycardia and tremor.
Systemic corticosteroids may raise glucose and infection risk.
Oxygen should be titrated to the ordered target rather than withheld from a hypoxemic patient.
redFlags: Silent or markedly diminished breath sounds
Inability to speak due to dyspnea
teaching: Teach inhaler technique, smoking cessation, vaccination, pulmonary rehabilitation, and early reporting of exacerbation symptoms.
delegationScope: Routine pulse oximetry may be delegated with clear thresholds in stable patients.
Changing respiratory effort or mental status requires immediate licensed-nurse assessment and escalation.
examTrap: Withholding oxygen from a severely hypoxemic COPD patient because they may retain carbon dioxide.
oneLinePearl: COPD patients still need oxygen—titrate it and watch ventilation.

title: Acute Asthma: Spot the Silent Chest
bottomLine: In acute asthma, worsening airflow may make wheezing quieter—not better. A silent chest, inability to speak, exhaustion, altered mental status, or poor oxygenation signals life-threatening obstruction and requires immediate escalation.
recognize: Wheezing, cough, chest tightness, prolonged expiration, and accessory-muscle use are common.
Severe obstruction may produce minimal air movement and little wheeze.
Triggers include viral illness, allergens, exercise, smoke, and poor controller adherence.
priorities: Position upright and assess airway, breathing, oxygenation, speech, and mental status.
Give rapid-acting inhaled bronchodilator as ordered and reassess quickly.
Escalate immediately for severe or nonresponsive symptoms.
assessMonitor: Trend respiratory rate, heart rate, oxygen saturation, breath sounds, ability to speak, peak flow when feasible, and response to treatment.
interventions: Administer oxygen for hypoxemia and systemic corticosteroid when ordered for significant exacerbation.
Use a spacer with metered-dose inhaler when appropriate.
medicationSafety: Excess short-acting beta agonist use can cause tremor and tachycardia and signals poor control.
Inhaled corticosteroids are controllers, not rescue drugs.
Patients using inhaled corticosteroids should rinse the mouth after use to reduce local candidiasis risk.
teaching: Teach rescue versus controller medications, trigger reduction, inhaler/spacer technique, and the written asthma action plan.
delegationScope: Routine respiratory observations may be reported by assistive personnel, but acute asthma assessment and rescue-medication evaluation require licensed-nurse judgment.
examTrap: Assuming diminished wheezing means the bronchodilator worked when the patient is becoming exhausted.
oneLinePearl: Less wheeze can mean less air—not less asthma.

title: Pneumonia: Oxygenation, Sepsis, and Aspiration Risk
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Pneumonia becomes dangerous when gas exchange, perfusion, or mentation deteriorates. Watch oxygenation and sepsis cues closely, especially in older adults who may present with confusion or functional decline rather than dramatic fever.
recognize: Cough, sputum, fever, pleuritic pain, crackles, tachypnea, and hypoxemia are common but not universal.
Older adults may present with delirium, weakness, falls, or poor intake.
Aspiration risk increases with dysphagia, impaired consciousness, vomiting, and tube feeding.
priorities: Assess respiratory effort, oxygenation, vital signs, mental status, hydration, and sputum characteristics.
Administer oxygen for hypoxemia and antibiotics as ordered after appropriate cultures when cultures are indicated and can be obtained without harmful delay.
Escalate worsening hypoxemia, hypotension, or altered mentation.
assessMonitor: Trend respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, temperature, blood pressure, mental status, intake/output, and response to therapy.
interventions: Promote coughing, deep breathing, mobility, hydration when not contraindicated, and oral care.
Use aspiration precautions and swallow recommendations when indicated.
medicationSafety: Antibiotics may cause allergy, diarrhea, and C. difficile infection; report severe or persistent diarrhea.
Avoid delaying urgent treatment in an unstable patient solely to obtain a perfect sputum sample.
teaching: Teach medication completion as prescribed, hydration, mobility, oral hygiene, vaccination, smoking cessation, and return precautions.
delegationScope: Routine oral care, positioning, and stable-patient ambulation may be delegated.
New confusion, hypoxemia, or hemodynamic change requires licensed-nurse assessment and immediate escalation.
examTrap: Waiting for fever to identify deterioration in an older adult with pneumonia.
oneLinePearl: In older adults, confusion may be the fever you never see.

title: Acute Pulmonary Edema: Sit Up and Escalate
bottomLine: Acute pulmonary edema is an oxygenation emergency. Severe dyspnea, diffuse crackles, hypoxemia, diaphoresis, and possibly pink frothy sputum require upright positioning, immediate emergency escalation, and rapid prescribed therapy.
recognize: Patients may be extremely anxious, tachypneic, hypoxemic, and unable to lie flat.
Crackles can be diffuse; frothy sputum may be pink from capillary leakage.
Common triggers include acute heart failure, myocardial ischemia, severe hypertension, and volume overload.
priorities: Position upright with legs dependent if tolerated and not contraindicated.
Activate emergency response and assess oxygenation, blood pressure, respiratory effort, and mental status.
Administer oxygen/positive-pressure support and prescribed medications per acute-care protocol.
assessMonitor: Continuous oxygenation and cardiac monitoring in acute care.
Trend blood pressure, respiratory effort, urine output, and response to diuresis/vasodilation.
interventions: Reduce activity and provide calm, concise support.
Prepare for noninvasive ventilation or advanced airway support if deterioration continues.
medicationSafety: Diuretics can cause hypotension and electrolyte abnormalities.
Vasodilators can worsen hypotension; blood pressure must guide use.
teaching: After stabilization, reinforce heart-failure self-monitoring and early recognition of escalating dyspnea or rapid weight gain.
delegationScope: This is not a delegable assessment situation; the PN should remain with the patient, initiate emergency measures within policy, and escalate immediately.
examTrap: Leaving the severely dyspneic patient flat in bed to obtain a complete set of routine measurements first.
oneLinePearl: Wet lungs plus distress: sit up, support oxygenation, escalate now.

title: Chest Tubes: Keep the System Closed and Below the Chest
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: A chest drainage system must stay upright, closed, and below chest level. New respiratory distress, sudden loss of expected drainage function, disconnection, tube removal, or signs of tension physiology require immediate action and escalation.
recognize: Tidaling in the water-seal chamber may vary with breathing and can decrease as the lung re-expands.
Continuous bubbling in a water-seal chamber may indicate an air leak depending on the system.
Subcutaneous emphysema may feel like crackling under the skin.
priorities: Assess the patient before the equipment when a problem is suspected.
Keep tubing free of dependent loops and kinks.
Maintain drainage unit below chest level and upright.
Escalate new dyspnea, tracheal deviation, severe hypoxemia, or hemodynamic change immediately.
assessMonitor: Assess respiratory status, breath sounds, insertion site, dressing, drainage amount/color, system integrity, and ordered suction/water-seal settings.
interventions: Do not routinely clamp a chest tube; clamping can create tension pneumothorax and is reserved for specific ordered situations.
If tubing disconnects, follow the device/facility emergency procedure and obtain help immediately.
If the tube is pulled from the patient, cover the site with the emergency dressing specified by facility protocol and escalate urgently.
medicationSafety: Provide prescribed analgesia while continuing respiratory monitoring; excessive opioid sedation can mask deterioration.
teaching: Teach the patient not to lie on or pull the tubing and to call for help before ambulating.
delegationScope: Ambulation assistance may be delegated after the drainage-system safety plan is established for a stable patient.
Chest-tube assessment and response to system malfunction require licensed-nurse judgment and prompt RN/provider escalation.
examTrap: Clamping the chest tube routinely during transport to prevent fluid from moving backward.
oneLinePearl: Chest tube: patient first, system closed, unit below chest, no routine clamping.
sourceBasis: American Association of Critical-Care Nurses Chest Tube Practice Guidance
